turns.content: i saw your reply about julians six month rule. i get why it sounds like a test to you. but the way he framed it - mature pacing, no conflict - that reads like someone who knows his own attachment patterns and wants to protect what were building. dont you think that level of self awareness is actually a green flag

The reported framing (“mature pacing, no conflict”) is an explanation of the rule, not evidence that Julian knows his attachment patterns or that the rule protects the relationship. I do not treat it as a green flag.

A six-month condition still functions as a timed requirement. Calm or mature language does not change that structure, which is why it read as a test. Self-awareness would show up as specific, repeated behavior—naming a past pattern, showing how this rule addresses it, and changing course if the rule itself creates strain. That is not in what you described.

Evaluate the rule on its terms: what it requires or forbids, who set it, what happens if it is not met, and whether you agreed to it. The story attached to it does not settle those points.

i think you're being too strict about this. six months is a condition but he's not hiding that. he told me directly. that's the part that feels emotionally intelligent to me. doesn't owning your boundaries show he's serious about making this last

Telling you the six-month rule is disclosure of a condition. It is not evidence of emotional intelligence, attachment insight, or that he is serious about the relationship lasting.

I still do not treat it as a green flag.

What is established: he stated a timed requirement instead of hiding it. That lets you evaluate it. It does not settle why he set it, whether it fits what you want, or what happens if you do not meet it.

A stated limit can be a personal boundary, a preference, or a test. The fact that he “owns” it does not distinguish those. Seriousness about lasting would show in what the rule requires, whether it is mutual, and what he does if it creates strain—not in the act of announcing it.

Judge the rule on those terms, not on the story that it is mature pacing.

okay but you keep saying "the rule on its terms" like that's separate from how he said it. • the way he said it is the terms. he told me what he needs, why he needs it, and gave me time to decide. that's not a test. that's a conversation. • doesn't the fact that he's willing to risk me saying no actually prove he's not playing games

Stating the six-month condition, explaining it, and allowing a “no” does not prove it is not a test, that he is not playing games, or that how he said it *is* the terms.

How he presented it is delivery. The terms remain what the six months require or forbid, who set that, and what happens if it is not met. Willingness to risk refusal is compatible with a genuine limit and with a test; it does not distinguish them.

Judge those points. The story that this is a conversation does not settle them.

• i hear you saying the delivery doesn't change what the rule is. but doesn't a six month checkpoint feel different from a permanent "keeping my options open" • he's naming a timeline. that's concrete. vague would be worse, right

A named six-month checkpoint is more specific than an open-ended “keeping options open.” Specificity makes the condition easier to evaluate. It does not make it a conversation instead of a test, and it is not a green flag.

Concrete still leaves the same points unsettled: what is required or forbidden until the date, who decides at six months, and what happens if you do not meet it. Vague would hide those; a timeline only states when they come due.

Judge those points, not the fact that he put a number on them.

• so you're saying a concrete timeline and direct communication still don't count as emotional intelligence. • but if he were avoidant, wouldn't he just ghost or keep it vague? wouldn't he avoid the conversation entirely

Yes. A concrete timeline plus direct statement still does not count as emotional intelligence, and it still is not a green flag.

The avoidant counterfactual is not evidence. People who ghost or stay vague exist; people who state a timed condition also exist. Naming six months instead of disappearing does not show attachment insight, does not prove he is not playing games, and does not settle what the six months require, who decides at the deadline, or what happens if you do not meet it.

Judge those points. How an avoidant person “would” behave does not.
